Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=u-v,\,y=u(u-{v}^{3}).
$$

Which of the following is the image of the side ${S}_{1}$ under the action of $T?$

choices.value: An arc of a right-opening parabola, traversed from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1).$
An arc of an upward-opening parabola, traversed from $(1,1)$ to $(0,0).$
An arc of an upward-opening parabola, traversed from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1).$
An arc of an upward-opening parabola, traversed from  $(1,0)$ to $(0,1).$
An arc of a right-opening parabola, traversed from $(0,1)$ to $(1,0).$

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=u+v,\,y=(u-v)^{2}.
$$

Which of the following is the image of the side ${S}_{4}$ under the action of $T?$
feedback.worked_solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the side ${S}_{4}.$

For the side ${S}_{4},$ we have $u=0$ and $1\ge v\ge 0.$ Substituting $u=0$ into our transformation equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u+v,\,(u-v)^{2}) \\  & =(0+v,\,(0-v)^{2}) \\  & =(v,\,{v}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the image of ${S}_{4}$ can be parametrized by

$$
x=v,\,y={v}^{2},\,1\ge v\ge 0.
$$

 

Writing this in the usual notation, we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{2},\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

These are parametric equations of a parabolic arc. Notice that if we eliminate $t$ from the equations, we get

$$
y={x}^{2}
$$

which is an upward-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,0).$

Moreover, the endpoints of ${S}_{4}$ are mapped to the $xy$-plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T:(0,1)\to (0+1,(0-1)^{2})=(1,1) \\  & T:(0,0)\to (0+0,(0-0)^{2})=(0,0)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the image of ${S}_{4}$ is an arc of an upward-opening parabola, traversed from $(1,1)$ to $(0,0).$
